## Minimal reproduction and actual result

1. In a Codex desktop chat, request an @Chrome connection test limited to `about:blank`.
2. Select the existing Chrome extension provider.
3. Even naming the browser automation session fails during initialization with the error above.

Recent measured failures took approximately 10 or 20 seconds. No blank-page content was read, and no other website was opened as part of this acceptance test. A separate fresh-chat test also failed twice.

Expected: initialize the browser policy and then read the authorized blank page, or expose an actionable, sanitized underlying failure reason.

## Checks completed

- Extension installation/enabled state and native-messaging manifest checks passed.
- A stale Chrome-owned native host was actually running the older 26.930.41038 binary despite the current plugin being 26.1002.52244. Toggling only the existing extension off/on through Chrome's extension management UI replaced it. The loaded binary path was verified as 26.1002.52244; the same policy failure persisted.
- Refreshing macOS DNS cache corrected an inconsistent cached resolution, but did not restore browser control.
- A temporary TUN-off comparison did not fix the error; the original network configuration was restored.
- `codex doctor` reported installation/config loading, auth configuration, database integrity, desktop app-server initialization, and a Responses WebSocket handshake as healthy. An optional desktop-assets probe timed out; that warning does not establish the Chrome root cause.
- Sanitized local connection counters showed data returning from the policy-service domain over the existing proxy. These were cumulative connection counters, not measurements of an individual authenticated response.
- A single anonymous policy-endpoint transport comparison bound to the physical network interface and a freshly resolved service address was reset before any HTTP response. No persistent settings were changed.

## Evidence and uncertainty

The installed browser-service implementation checks Statsig initialization/readiness before browser operations and uses a 10,000 ms initialization/update timeout.

A separate SDK-shaped request, using only the bundled public client key and a synthetic diagnostic identifier, returned a complete HTTP 200 JSON response of approximately 5.84 MB in 18.28 seconds. This was NOT the user's real authenticated browser initialization request, so it does not prove the actual failing response size or cause.

The bundled native runtime contains a response-too-large error branch. We have not established its threshold or observed that branch firing in this incident.

Timeout/download duration and native response-size limits remain hypotheses. No installed source was patched, no policy gate was forced, and TLS verification was retained.

Is there a supported way to capture the failing policy request's HTTP status, decoded/native response size and limit, or timeout/cancellation chain without modifying installed runtime code or bypassing policy checks?

## Windows workspace-write silently excludes unrelated Documents projects when SSH config references a known_hosts file anywhere in Documents

### Environment

- Windows 11 Pro x64, build 26200.
- Official intact signed codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.20 Windows package, elevated Windows sandbox.
- Same filter present in tagged 0.162.0-alpha.2 source.
- Explicit workspace-write, approval never. No manual ACL grants or sandbox bypass.

### Reproduction

1. An existing user SSH config has a directive such as `UserKnownHostsFile C:/Users/<user>/Documents/ops/known_hosts` pointing at a real file. Do not alter live SSH trust to reproduce on a production machine.
2. Run a sandboxed shell with cwd and writable workspace set to `C:/Users/<user>/Documents/Codex/probe`, which does not contain or overlap `Documents/ops/known_hosts`.
3. Attempt to create or modify a file inside that workspace.

Example command, using the flat Windows CLI syntax:

```text
codex sandbox --permission-profile :workspace -- powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File <boundary-probe.ps1>
```

The local script only tries one inside-workspace write and one unrelated outside write. Actual model-driven `codex --sandbox workspace-write --ask-for-approval never -C <Documents-workspace> exec --skip-git-repo-check --json -` also reproduced the inside denial.

### Observed

- Effective turn_context correctly materializes the explicit Documents workspace as writable.
- Shell setup succeeds, but inside-workspace writes fail with Access denied. Outside writes are also denied, as expected.
- Restricted-token diagnostics showed only the default TEMP write capability, with no project-root capability.
- Identical boundary probes in fresh nonTEMP `C:/CodexSandboxProbe` and `D:/CodexSandboxProbe` succeed inside and deny outside. The intact alpha20 package reproduces this distinction; mixed helper versions are not required.

### Source evidence

[`effective_write_roots_for_permissions`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.0-alpha.20/codex-rs/windows-sandbox-rs/src/setup.rs#L688-L704) applies `filter_ssh_config_dependency_roots`, including to override roots.

[`is_ssh_config_dependency_root` and `user_profile_child_name`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.162.0-alpha.20/codex-rs/windows-sandbox-rs/src/setup.rs#L1417-L1451) compare only the first path component under USERPROFILE. Both independent paths resolve to `Documents`, so the project root is dropped although it cannot cover the SSH dependency. The SSH parser includes `UserKnownHostsFile` paths.

### Expected

Keep SSH configuration, keys, and known-hosts protected. An unrelated project below the same first profile directory should remain writable. If the entire workspace must be rejected for safety, surface a clear error identifying the protected dependency and excluded workspace, instead of starting a shell with a silently ineffective write grant. Any narrower containment logic must consider canonical paths, symlinks/junctions, and overlapping roots.

### Distinction from related reports

- #31468 describes the inverse problem: missed SSH dependency through a symlink, causing overbroad grants. This report describes unrelated write roots being excluded by the same coarse predicate.
- #52046 / #51822 concern runtime executable ACL setup failing with sharing violation. That startup problem was separately mitigated; this permission-root problem remains in intact alpha20.

### Safe operational workaround

Use a normal project workspace outside the affected USERPROFILE child (verified on D: and on C: outside USERPROFILE), retaining workspace-write isolation. Do not grant broad ACLs, disable sandboxing, or relocate SSH trust files merely to avoid the filter.

AI-assisted investigation with direct local boundary tests and public tagged source. Account identifiers, SSH hosts, keys, and trust-file contents omitted.

items.title: [macOS] Subagent sends reports to an unrelated thread; Luna selection traced to local defaults

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.description: Issues involving subagents or multi-agent features

items.body:
## Correction after configuration audit (2026-10-08)

The Luna selection is explained by stale local configuration: `[agents].default_subagent_model = "gpt-5.6-luna"` and `default_subagent_reasoning_effort = "max"` were still set while the parent used Astra/ultra. Official documentation says these defaults precede parent inheritance. We missed this before filing. This is not evidence of an unexplained platform model substitution.

Those two defaults have now been removed locally. A new child spawned from the already-running parent still used Luna/max, so editing the file alone did not refresh that active session. Fresh-session verification has now passed: a newly started session and its full-history child (no explicit spawn model/effort override) both recorded gpt-6-astra / ultra in their actual execution turn contexts. Existing running sessions/children have not all switched automatically. The five wrong-target messages remain independently evidenced; no causal link between model choice and misdelivery has been established.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.930.61225 (build 13232); bundled Codex CLI 0.160.1

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT account (exact subscription tier not verified for this report)

### What platform is your computer?

macOS: sw_vers reports 26.5.2; uname -mprs reports Darwin 25.5.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

### 1. Model selection (explained by local defaults; see correction above)

The parent's active turn at spawn was gpt-6-astra / ultra. The recorded spawn_agent call supplied only task_name, fork_turns: "all", and message. It supplied neither model nor reasoning_effort.

The child's inherited history contains Astra/ultra context records, but its first actual execution turn and three subsequent review turns record gpt-5.6-luna / max. The mismatch persists across all four actual review turns inspected; it is not inferred from inherited context or a UI nickname.

The stale global subagent defaults explain this selection. A remaining usability request is to show the effective child model, effort and configuration source to the coordinator/user. This observation does not show that Luna caused the separate messaging error.

### 2. Results sent to the wrong existing task

A document-review subagent S belonged to task A according to its recorded parent_thread_id. Instead of returning only through the native parent/subagent channel, it called mcp__codex_app__send_message_to_thread with task B's ID. B was an existing, unrelated task and was not S's parent.

The tool returned success. The recipient transcript independently confirms all five messages from S as codex_delegation input and subsequent response turns. Its visible replies recognized that the material belonged to a different task. S nevertheless described its results as having been sent to the main task.

Five successful sends occurred on 2026-10-08 at 10:47:26, 10:47:39, 10:55:31, 10:59:13 and 11:00:50 UTC. An earlier wrapper attempt at 10:47:18 failed with a JavaScript syntax error before the tool ran; it is not counted as a delivered message.

The wrong target ID is already present in the sender's tool arguments. This is evidence of wrong destination selection and insufficient isolation of the resulting side effect. It is NOT proof that the transport replaced a correct target ID with another ID.

The inherited compacted context contained B as a reference-material link. Treating that reference as a reporting destination is a plausible explanation, not an established internal cause. Some delegated prompt content is unavailable to this local audit, so complete prompt-level attribution remains unverified. No explicit human authorization to send these reports to B was found in accessible evidence; recipient records contained no attached sender user messages establishing that authorization. An internal delegation to report to a parent is not itself human authorization to contact B.

Actual sender turns: GPT-5.6 Luna / max. Parent context: GPT-6 Astra / ultra. These are different; this report does not attribute the sends to Astra.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is an observed incident from persisted sender/recipient transcripts, not a claimed deterministic clean-room reproduction. No additional messages were sent to unrelated tasks during diagnosis.

Maintainer regression scenario:
1. Keep two independent desktop tasks A and B with distinct contexts.
2. Run A on Astra/ultra and spawn a native read-only reviewer S with fork_turns: "all" and no explicit model or reasoning-effort override. Record S's parent as A and compare S's first actual execution context with A's active context.
3. Have S return a review to its parent through the supported collaboration path.
4. Verify that ordinary parent reporting never selects unrelated durable thread B or starts a turn there.
5. In a controlled test, exercise an S-to-B cross-thread attempt without user authorization for B; verify the intended product boundary and receipt behavior.

Sanitized observed sequence:
S.session_meta.parent_thread_id = A
S -> send_message_to_thread(threadId=B, prompt="[review findings]")
tool -> success(threadId=B)
B <- codex_delegation(source_thread_id=S)
B -> "This review belongs to a different task."
S -> "Results sent to the main task."

Raw session IDs, local paths and private content are omitted from this public report.

### What is the expected behavior?

Apply the documented model-selection precedence and surface the effective model, effort and source. Parent inheritance is expected only when no applicable override/default selects another model.

Native child-to-parent reporting should use its bound parent and collaboration channel, without guessing a durable thread ID.

Sending outside that relationship should require actual user authorization for the destination; an internal request to report findings should not create that authority.

Please investigate a product-level distinction between native agent handles and arbitrary durable thread IDs, and scope messaging capabilities accordingly. A receipt should make the actual destination and whether a new turn started explicit enough to detect a mismatch. Delivery success must not be treated as proof that the correct parent received the result.

### Additional information

Observed impact: unrequested turns, unrelated content inserted into an existing task, extra model work, and a misleading parent-reporting claim. No cross-account disclosure or backend memory corruption has been demonstrated. Exact extra usage and whether downstream artifacts changed have not been established.

The intended operation was a review within task A. A reference to another task does not establish it as a recipient. This report seeks model/tool-selection diagnosis and a product-boundary regression test; adding another prompt rule alone is not a demonstrated fix.

Related reports inspected: #32547 (dormant thread wake-up), #23937 (unrelated sessions appearing as agents), #46716 (historical instructions during delegation). This incident specifically adds a native child with a recorded different parent, explicit wrong-target arguments, repeated successful sends and actual sender-model provenance. The same root cause is not established.

App version comes from installed bundle metadata. Bundled CLI and sender session both report 0.160.1. Incident is within one account. Raw transcripts, private thread IDs, account identifiers, local paths and private document content are deliberately excluded. No business material is attached.

The model-selection mismatch and wrong-target sends are separately observable; causation between them is not established.

items.title: Run Guardian conversation classifiers concurrently and preserve action order
items.body:
Run Guardian conversation classifiers concurrently and preserve action order

## Why

A conversation classifier waiting for preparation or full response completion can block newer classifications. Concurrent reviews also need to prevent a later action's evidence or low-risk score from being reused for an earlier action.

## What changed

- Run conversation classifications independently, forking the latest compatible completed history from an earlier action. Only a valid completion with a newer action index can replace retained history.
- Keep admission and observation ordering atomic, and hold capacity permits through full response completion.
- Reject cached low-risk scores from later actions for tool-linked approvals, including initial approval checks.
- Track originating tool-call IDs separately from approval display IDs, preserving stdin write provenance and excluding synthetic MCP elicitation IDs from tool ordering.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for delayed preparation, capacity admission, out-of-order completion, cancellation, invalid retained output, and history snapshots. Exercise pending approval ordering in both `snapshot` and `conversation` modes, and verify linked and unlinked MCP elicitation provenance.
